verses.text: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
verses.context: In Matthew 11:25-30, Jesus speaks about knowing the Father, then invites those who are weary to come to him. Read the next two verses too: the invitation continues with learning from his gentleness and humility.
verses.title: You do not have to carry it all.
verses.reflection: An invitation to bring what is heavy, without first making it presentable.
verses.simple: You can come to God tired, unfinished, and carrying more than you know how to hold. You do not have to earn the right to rest.
verses.meaning: The passage moves from coming to Jesus to learning his way. Rest is connected with a relationship and a different way of carrying life, rather than a promise that every responsibility immediately disappears.
verses.theology: A Christian reading finds both grace and discipleship here: an invitation is offered before a person has solved their burdens, and it leads into learning from Jesus. The following image of a yoke connects rest with following his teaching.
verses.today: Notice one burden you could name honestly. Rest might begin with a pause, a prayer, or asking someone for practical help. Those actions are reflections on the passage, not requirements for receiving care.
verses.question: What am I carrying that I could share with someone today?

verses.text: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.
verses.context:
John 13 to 17 takes place on the last night of the life of Jesus, at supper and just after. Judas has gone out. Jesus has told the others that he is leaving them, and they are full of sorrow. Much of chapter 14 is his comfort for them.

The chapter opens with the words, Do not let your heart be troubled, and this verse repeats them, now that he has given them reasons. In between he speaks of the Father’s house, of himself as the way, and of the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, who will teach them and remind them of all he said.

Even after all this, the disciples are still troubled. They are thinking of the hard days ahead and of losing him. Their fear comes partly from love and partly from alarm.
verses.title: Peace, even in uncertainty.
verses.reflection: Words spoken into uncertainty, rather than from the other side of it.
verses.simple:
On the night before he dies, Jesus says goodbye to his friends. The gift he leaves them is peace, and not just any peace. He calls it my peace.

This is not the polite peace people wish each other at the door. It is a real gift, and the world can neither give it nor take it away. So he tells them, as he did at the start of the evening, not to let their hearts be troubled or afraid.

He is going away, but he is not leaving them with nothing.
verses.meaning:
Peace here is more than a calm feeling. It stands for every good thing Jesus gives: peace with God, peace with one another, and a quiet heart that knows it has been forgiven.

Not as the world gives. When people wish each other peace, it is often a formality, or a wish they cannot make come true. The peace of Jesus is not an empty wish. It comes with the thing itself. The gifts of the world touch only the body and this life, and what the world gives, it can take back. His peace reaches the soul and lasts. The peace of the world is unsettled and soon gone. His fills the soul with a steady quiet.

Troubled and afraid. The two words look in two directions. The heart is troubled by what has already happened, and afraid of what may still come. Jesus speaks to both.
verses.theology:
Christ himself is our peace. What Jesus leaves with his friends as he goes to the Father is his own presence, which he never takes away. Scripture calls him our peace. He left their sight, but his presence in their hearts did not change. They would miss his bodily presence, yet they would have him truly with them through the Spirit.

This peace begins with God. Christ made peace through the blood of his cross and reconciled people to God. Peace with one another and a quiet mind flow from that. Catholic teaching adds that every peace on earth is an image and a fruit of the peace of Christ.

It is peace for troubled times. Jesus does not promise his friends an easy road. Early Christian preachers heard him saying that the trouble of the world cannot harm those who are at peace with him, and that being at peace with one another makes them stronger. He gives this peace to people who will face trouble and need it.

Our peace now is real but not yet full. In this life we still pray, Forgive us our debts, and we never fully see into one another’s hearts. So Christians hold on to the peace they have now, while longing for the peace to come, which nothing will disturb.
verses.today: If something is troubling you or making you afraid, you might name it quietly to Jesus today, just as it is. Then sit for a moment with his words, Peace I leave with you. There is no need to feel calm first.
verses.question: What would it be like to receive peace today, rather than trying to make it myself?

words.meaning: The Greek word for peace carries the Hebrew sense Jesus shared: welfare and well-being. People wished it on each other when they met and when they parted, so these words are also his farewell. What others could only wish, he actually gives.

echoes.text: “Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me.
echoes.note: Jesus began the evening with the same words, and now repeats them because he has given his friends reason to believe them.

echoes.text: For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,
echoes.note: The peace Jesus leaves is himself: he is our peace, who made both one.

echoes.text: “Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men.”
echoes.note: The same peace the angels announced at his birth is the gift he leaves at his parting.

echoes.text: For a child is born to us. A son is given to us; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
echoes.note: The peace of Christ is the peace of the promised Prince of Peace.

echoes.text: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
echoes.note: Our peace in this life is real but not complete, which is why we still pray to be forgiven.

teaching.title: Christ himself is our peace
teaching.text: What Jesus leaves as he goes to the Father is his own presence, which he never withdraws. He is our peace, who made both one. He left the sight of his friends, but not their hearts. They would lack only his bodily presence, and would have him truly through the Spirit.

teaching.title: This peace begins with God
teaching.text: The peace Jesus gives is first of all peace with God, then peace with one another and a quiet mind. Christ made peace through the blood of his cross and reconciled people to God. Catholic teaching calls all peace on earth an image and fruit of the peace of Christ, the Prince of Peace.

teaching.title: It is peace for troubled times
teaching.text: Jesus does not promise his friends that trouble will stay away. The trouble of the world cannot harm those who are at peace with him, and being at peace with one another makes them stronger. He gives this peace to people who will be exposed to trouble and need it. It is not a mere formality but a real blessing.

teaching.title: Our peace now is real but not yet full
teaching.text: The peace we have in this life is mixed. We still pray to be forgiven, and we never see fully into one another’s hearts. Christians hold on to the peace they have here, while longing for the peace of the life to come, which nothing will disturb.

differences.title: Two gifts, or one said twice?
differences.text: Some read peace and my peace as two gifts: the peace Jesus leaves with us in this world, and his own full peace, which he will give in the world to come. Others take the second phrase as a simple repeat of the first. The early preacher who raised the question left his hearers free to read it either way.

differences.title: Where the traditions put the weight
differences.text: Early Christian preaching in Greek stresses peace with Christ and with one another as a source of courage in danger. Catholic teaching sets the peace of Christ at the root of all peace on earth, and calls peace the work of justice and the effect of love. Protestant writers stress the quiet of a mind that knows it is forgiven. These are differences of emphasis, not of doctrine.

verses.text: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.
verses.context: Romans 15 asks a diverse community to welcome one another. In verses 7-12, Paul brings together passages about the nations praising God. This prayer follows that picture of people sharing in hope.
verses.title: A little room for hope.
verses.reflection: A prayer for hope that can be received, rather than manufactured.
verses.simple: Hope does not always begin as a big feeling. This is a prayer that joy and peace can grow in you, even when you cannot make them happen on your own.
verses.meaning: Paul asks the God of hope to fill people with joy and peace. The prayer is addressed to a community, so its horizon includes life with other people as well as individual experience.
verses.theology: The verse names God, belief, and the power of the Holy Spirit. Many Christians read it as a picture of hope sustained by divine action, lived within a welcoming community.
verses.today: A small step toward hope might be accepting company, noticing something good, or allowing another person to hope alongside you. The prayer need not become pressure to feel joyful immediately.
verses.question: What is one small thing I can still hope for today?

verses.text: In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
verses.context: Near the end of 1 Thessalonians, Paul gives a series of short instructions for community life. Verses 16-18 place rejoicing, prayer, and thanksgiving together. Read them alongside the call to encourage and help one another.
verses.title: Let the good things count.
verses.reflection: Gratitude can notice what is good without denying what is difficult.
verses.simple: You can notice a small good thing even on a complicated day. Gratitude does not mean pretending that everything that happened was good.
verses.meaning: The wording says to give thanks in everything. It can be read as a practice within changing circumstances, rather than an instruction to call every harmful event good.
verses.theology: The phrase in Christ Jesus locates thanksgiving within Christian life and relationship with God. Gratitude is held alongside ongoing prayer and the care of a community, rather than presented as a technique for controlling outcomes.
verses.today: Name something specific: a person, a moment, or a kindness. You can be grateful and still grieve, ask for help, or work to change something unjust.
verses.question: What small kindness would I like to remember from today?

verses.text: Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.
verses.context:
These words belong to the last long talk Jesus gives his disciples, at the close of the Last Supper, on the night he is betrayed. At the end of chapter 14 he says, Get up, let us go from here. Then he speaks of himself as the true vine, with his Father as the gardener and his disciples as the branches.

Chapter 15 moves through four themes: fruit, love, the hatred of the world, and the coming Comforter. This verse opens the part about love, verses 9 to 17, which leads to the command to love one another.

Jesus is about to leave. His friends could be tempted to drift away from him, and to grow distant from one another. They might also feel abandoned, as if he were sending them into a hostile world and walking away. So he tells them where they stand.
verses.title: There is room for you here.
verses.reflection: Love comes before the invitation to remain in it.
verses.simple:
Jesus tells his friends how he loves them: in the same way the Father loves him. Then he asks them to stay in that love, to make their home there and not wander off.

The love comes first. They do not earn it. It is already given, and they are invited to remain in it, the way a branch stays joined to the vine.

He says this as he is about to leave them. He is not going because he loves them less.
verses.meaning:
As the Father has loved me. Jesus is not saying that our nature is equal to his. He speaks as the one who stands between God and us. The love of God was poured out on him so that from him it might flow to all who belong to him. In him, as in a mirror, we can see the Father’s love for us.

So I have loved you. The Father loved the Son, who was most worthy. Jesus loves his friends, who are least worthy. What the Father has given him, he passes on to them. It is a love that chose to die even for those who were his enemies.

Remain in my love. Since he has just spoken of his love for them, this is first of all his love for them. To remain in it is to keep your place in his affection, to go on living in his grace and not throw it away. Older English Bibles say continue or abide.
verses.theology:
God’s love reaches us through Christ. Christians have long taught that we do not find the love of God by searching on our own. Trying to do so is like entering a maze with no way in or out. We look to Christ, the beloved Son. The Father loves us too, but in him.

Love comes first, and obedience follows. The next verse links remaining in his love with keeping his commandments. Yet keeping them does not win his love. Unless he loves us, we cannot keep them at all. Our obedience is the fruit of his love, not its cause. We love because we were first loved.

We stay by asking to be kept. Jesus speaks to his friends as people who are able to stay, and he warns them not to lose so great a gift. Yet we do not stay by our own strength. We pray to the one who gives the command, that he will keep us in his love.

His love holds in hard times. Jesus points to himself. The Father loves him, and still he will suffer. Suffering is not a sign that we are unloved. This love also overflows. Catholic teaching calls it the new commandment: loving one another, the disciples copy the love they themselves receive.
verses.today: Before you do anything else today, you might take a quiet moment simply to be loved. Picture a branch resting on the vine, held rather than holding on. If it helps, ask him in a few plain words to keep you in his love.
verses.question: Where am I still trying to earn a place that has already been given to me?

echoes.text: We love him, because he first loved us.
echoes.note: John says the same thing in his letter: our love springs from his love, which came first.

echoes.text: Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
echoes.note: The Father calls Jesus his beloved Son, and in him we see the Father’s love for us.

echoes.text: to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he freely gave us favor in the Beloved.
echoes.note: The Father loves the Son so that in the Beloved he might accept us too.

echoes.text: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.
echoes.note: The love Jesus gives his friends becomes the pattern for how they love one another.

echoes.text: Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
echoes.note: By loving his own to the end, Jesus shows the love he receives from the Father.

teaching.title: God’s love reaches us through Christ
teaching.text: We should not try to learn how God loves us apart from Christ, which is like wandering in a maze. We look to him, the beloved Son, in whom the love of God was poured out so that it might flow to us. The Father loves us too, but in him. In Christ, as in a mirror, we see the love of the Father for us all.

teaching.title: Love comes first, and obedience follows
teaching.text: Remaining in his love is joined to keeping his commandments, yet love comes first. We do not keep his commandments to awaken his love; unless he loves us, we cannot keep them. Obedience is not the cause of his love but its effect. We love because we were first loved.

teaching.title: We stay by asking to be kept
teaching.text: Jesus tells his friends to continue in his love, because they are able to. He warns them not to lose such a gift, and not to fall from it by their own fault. Yet we do not stay by our own strength. We pray to the one who gives the command, that he will keep us in his love.

teaching.title: His love holds in hard times
teaching.text: Jesus points to himself: the Father loves him, yet he must still suffer. So his friends should not take hardship as a sign that they are unloved. If they remain in his love, the dangers ahead cannot harm that love. And the love they receive becomes the love they show one another.

differences.title: Whose love?
differences.text: Some read remain in my love as a call for the disciples to love one another. Others, with good reason, read it as the love of Christ for us, since he has just spoken of it. Some hold both together: keep up your love for him, and stay in his love for you.

differences.title: Can someone fall away from this love?
differences.text: Some Protestant teachers read the warning as a real one: a person could lose this blessing, or Jesus would not need to say it. Others stress that we hold on only because God holds us, and so we pray for him to keep us. Both take the warning seriously and both look to grace.

differences.title: Where the traditions put the weight
differences.text: Early Christian preaching in Greek stresses comfort and courage: Jesus is not leaving because he loves them less. Catholic teaching hears the new commandment of love here, with joy, peace and mercy as its fruits. Protestant writers stress free grace in Christ, with obedience as its fruit. These are differences of emphasis, not of doctrine.

verses.text: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
verses.context: Psalm 34 is a song of thanksgiving, trust, and instruction. Its later verses acknowledge that righteous people still face troubles. Nearness to God is not presented as immunity from pain.
verses.title: Near to the brokenhearted.
verses.reflection: An assurance of nearness that makes room for grief.
verses.simple: A hurting heart is not a reason for God to turn away. This verse pictures God coming close to people who feel crushed.
verses.meaning: The parallel phrases broken heart and crushed spirit give language to deep distress. The verse emphasizes God’s nearness and care rather than blaming a person for suffering.
verses.theology: The psalm joins praise with the reality of affliction. Christians often read it as a witness to God’s presence in suffering. It does not require grief to disappear before a person can pray.
verses.today: You may sit with these words without trying to turn them into a positive feeling. Consider telling a trusted person what is difficult, or letting someone offer practical support.
verses.question: What would help me feel a little less alone with this?

verses.simple:
The Bible opens with one plain sentence: God created the heavens and the earth. Before we hear anything else, we learn who made all things, and that all things had a beginning.

The world did not make itself, and it is not the work of chance. It has a Maker, and it belongs to him. Everything else in Scripture rests on this first line, the way a house rests on its foundation.
verses.context:
This is the first verse of the Bible. It stands over the whole creation account like a heading, giving the entire work in one line. The next verse describes the earth before it was shaped. Then the days unfold one by one, and the account closes with God resting on the seventh day.

Early Christian preachers received this account as the work of Moses, the man who saw God face to face. The first three chapters of Genesis hold a special place. They were set at the very start of Scripture to teach the great truths about creation: where it comes from and where it is going, its order and goodness, our human calling, and the first sin with the hope of rescue that follows it.

The heavens and the earth means everything. By naming the highest and the lowest, the verse takes in all that lies between.
verses.meaning:
Every phrase in this verse carries weight. In the beginning means the beginning of time. Before it there was no one but God, who lives in eternity. Early Christian preachers noticed that these words come first for a reason: they shut the door on the idea that the world has always existed.

God is named at once, pressed into the reader’s heart like a seal, so that our own reasoning does not wander from the truth. The verb is chosen with care too. The writer does not say that God shaped or worked something already there. He says God created: what did not exist before now was. In the Bible this verb always has God as its subject.

Your Bible may word this verse a little differently. Orthodox Bibles, which follow the ancient Greek translation, say that God made the heaven and the earth. Others say created, and some say heaven where others say heavens. Each one points to the same thing: the whole of what exists, depending on the One who gives it being.
verses.theology:
The world had a beginning, and so did time. The world is not eternal. Time began together with heaven and earth, so there was no before in which God sat idle. And what began in time will one day end. These first words already point ahead to the world’s renewal.

God created freely, out of goodness. The world is not a shadow that falls from God without his choosing, and it is not the work of fate or chance. He made it because he willed to, out of love, to share his own being, wisdom and goodness. He gains nothing from it, yet everything comes from him and is meant for him.

God made all things through his Word. The New Testament reveals that the eternal Son was at work in this first act. Creation is the shared work of Father, Son and Spirit, and many have heard the Son in the word beginning itself.

Creation is the first step toward Christ. This verse is the foundation of all God’s saving plans. From the start, God had in view the new creation in Christ. Meanwhile the world itself is a school, where the things we can see lead us by the hand to the God we cannot see.
verses.today: Sometime today, pause over something ordinary: the sky, a tree, a glass of water. Remember that it had a beginning, and that it was made on purpose. If you like, say a quiet thank you to the One who began it all.
verses.question: What would change in my day if I trusted that the world, and my own life in it, began in God’s goodness?
verses.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
verses.title: In the beginning.
verses.reflection: Read the words slowly, in the passage around them.

words.meaning: The verb of creating. The writer did not use the ordinary word for shaping or forming something, but this one, which speaks of bringing into being what was not there before. In the Bible it always has God as its subject. Later in the chapter it returns for the great sea creatures and for human beings.
A plural form used for the one true God. Its short form, El, means the strong God, and only almighty strength could bring all things out of nothing.

echoes.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
echoes.note: John begins his Gospel with the same words and shows that all things were made through the Word.

echoes.text: By faith we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible.
echoes.note: By faith we understand that the world was made by the word of God, and that what is seen came from what does not appear.

echoes.text: For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him.
echoes.note: All things in heaven and on earth were created in the Son, through him and for him.

echoes.text: For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.
echoes.note: God’s unseen power is clearly seen through what he has made, so creation leads the mind to its Maker.

echoes.text: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
echoes.note: What had a beginning will also have an end: heaven and earth will pass away.

teaching.title: The world had a beginning, and so did time
teaching.text: Christians confess that the world is not eternal but was created by God. Time itself began together with heaven and earth. So it makes no sense to ask what God was doing for countless ages before, as if he waited: there was no then when there was no time. Early Christian preachers added a sober note. What began in time will also come to an end, and these short words already announce the end and the renewal of the world.

teaching.title: God created freely, out of goodness
teaching.text: The world is not a shadow that falls from God without his choosing, the way a body casts a shadow. Nor is it the product of necessity, blind fate or chance. God made it by his own free will, because he wanted his creatures to share in his being, wisdom and goodness. He has no other reason for creating than his love. He does not need our service, yet since all is of him, all must be for him.

teaching.title: God made all things through his Word
teaching.text: The New Testament reveals that God created everything through the eternal Word, his beloved Son, and the Church confesses the Spirit as the giver of life. Creation is the common work of Father, Son and Spirit. Early Christian prayer heard the Son even in the opening phrase: in the Beginning, that is, in his Word and Wisdom, God made heaven and earth. The Son, the eternal Wisdom of the Father, was with him when he made the world.

teaching.title: Creation is the first step toward Christ
teaching.text: Creation is the foundation of all God’s saving plans, the beginning of a history that reaches its height in Christ. From the very beginning God had in view the glory of the new creation in him. That is why the readings of the Easter Vigil begin with this account, and why in the Byzantine liturgy it is always the first reading at the vigils of the great feasts of the Lord. The world is also a school where we learn to know God, since the sight of visible things leads the mind, as by the hand, to the invisible.

differences.title: The beginning of time, or the Son?
differences.text: Some early and medieval teachers read the beginning in more than one way: as the beginning of time, and also as the Son, the Wisdom of God in whom all things were made. Others, among the Reformers, thought that applying this word to Christ goes beyond what the verse means, and read it plainly: at the start the world was not yet finished, but was made as raw material for all that followed. Both hold that the world was begun by the power of the Word.

differences.title: Does the plural name point to the Trinity?
differences.text: The Hebrew name for God here is plural in form. Some read in it a hint of Father, Son and Spirit, darkly shown in the Old Testament and clearly revealed in the New. Others warned against proving so great a truth from one word, and took the plural to express the powers God used in making the world. Both confess the Trinity. They differ only on what this one word can prove.

differences.title: All at once, or over six days?
differences.text: Some early preachers took the words in the beginning to mean a single, undivided moment, and taught that at God’s will the world arose in less than an instant. Others held that God really took six days, not because he needed them, but to suit his works to human understanding, so that we would stop and take in his glory.

verses.simple:
Before God says a single word, the Bible shows us what there was to work with: an earth with no shape and nothing living on it, deep water, and darkness everywhere.

This is not a picture of evil. It is a picture of a world that is not finished yet, still waiting to be made into a home. And it is not left alone. God’s Spirit is already there, hovering close over the water the way a bird hovers over its nest.

The very next thing God does is call light into being. So this verse is the moment just before. Nothing is finished, and God is already present.
verses.context:
The first verse of the Bible says everything in one line: God created the heavens and the earth. This verse slows down and describes the earth before God shaped it. Then the six days begin, as God calls light into being.

The verse names two things that are missing: the earth has no form, and it is empty. The six days answer them in that order. In the first three days God gives form: he separates light from dark, sky from sea, land from water. In the last three he fills what he has formed, with sun, moon and stars, birds and fish, animals and people. The great medieval account of the six days is built on this very pattern: a work of setting things apart, followed by a work of adorning them.

Israel’s neighbours also told creation stories that began with dark water. In one Babylonian story, the world is made after a war among the gods, out of the body of a goddess of the sea. Genesis uses a related word for the deep, but it tells a very different story. The deep is not a god. There is no battle, and nothing resists. There is one God, and he only has to speak.
verses.meaning:
The verse is honest about how creation begins: not with a finished world, but with raw material that is shapeless, dark and uninhabited. Yet Scripture never calls this state evil. An early Christian sermon on this verse rejected the idea that the darkness was an evil power at war with God. Darkness is simply air without light: the absence of light, not a rival to God.

And the raw material is not on its own. The Spirit of God is over it, quietly holding the unfinished world steady. The picture is of a mother bird hovering over her chicks to warm and cherish them, or covering her eggs and giving them life from her own warmth. This reading is very old, passed on by Christians whose own language was close to Hebrew.

Your Bible may word this verse differently. The ancient Greek translation, which Orthodox Bibles follow, describes the earth as invisible and unfurnished. The old Latin translation, behind Catholic English Bibles, calls it void and empty. That is why some early Christian writings speak of an invisible earth.
verses.theology:
God made everything, including the raw material. Christians of every tradition confess that God created out of nothing. This verse does not describe something that existed beside God from eternity. It describes the first state of what he had just made. If matter had always existed, it could claim the same honour as God. But God needs nothing already there, and no help, in order to create.

Father, Son and Spirit create together. Read with the rest of Scripture, the opening of Genesis shows the Father creating through his Word, with his Spirit over the waters. Christians have long seen the Trinity here: God the Creator, the Son as the Beginning in whom all things were made, and the Holy Spirit moving over the waters. God’s Word and his Breath stand at the origin of the being and life of every creature.

The Spirit gives life and holds creation in being. The hovering shows the Spirit preparing the waters to bring forth living things. And if even the first chaos needed God’s Spirit to keep it from falling apart, the ordered world needs him no less. Creation is not a machine that God started and left running.

The first creation points to the new creation. From early on, Christians saw baptism in this verse. The power that brought a world out of confusion, emptiness and darkness is the power that makes a person new, and that will one day raise the dead.
verses.today: Where is something in your life still formless or empty: a decision, a grief, a new start? This verse does not promise that it is finished. It says God is present over it before it is. Bring that one thing to him by name today.
verses.question: Where do I assume God only arrives once things are in order?
verses.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
verses.title: In the beginning.
verses.reflection: Read the words slowly, in the passage around them.

words.meaning: A rhyming pair: waste and emptiness, a place with no shape and nothing in it. The pair returns in Jeremiah 4:23, where the prophet sees the land undone by judgment. Isaiah 45:18 says God did not create the earth to be a waste, but formed it to be lived in: emptiness was never the goal.
The vast, deep sea. In the ancient world the sea stood for everything people could not control.
One Hebrew word means breath, wind and spirit. Most Christian Bibles translate it as the Spirit of God. Some modern and Jewish translations have a wind from God.
A rare verb. Its only other use in this form is Deuteronomy 32:11, where an eagle flutters over her young. It is the movement of a parent bird: close, protective and alive.

echoes.text: By the LORD’s word, the heavens were made: all their army by the breath of his mouth.
echoes.note: Word and breath (the same word, ruach) make the world together, just as in Genesis 1:2–3.

echoes.text: You send out your Spirit and they are created. You renew the face of the ground.
echoes.note: The Spirit’s work in creation did not stop on the first day.

echoes.text: I saw the earth and, behold, it was waste and void, and the heavens, and they had no light.
echoes.note: Sin drags the world back toward the emptiness of Genesis 1:2.

echoes.text: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
echoes.note: John retells the beginning with Jesus as the Word through whom all things were made.

echoes.text: Immediately coming up from the water, he saw the heavens parting and the Spirit descending on him like a dove.
echoes.note: At Jesus’ baptism the Spirit is over the water again, like a bird. A new creation is beginning.

echoes.text: …it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts…
echoes.note: Paul describes coming to faith as God doing Genesis 1 inside a person.

teaching.title: God made everything, including the raw material
teaching.text: Christians of every tradition confess that God created out of nothing. This verse does not describe something that existed beside God from eternity. It describes the first state of what he had just made. If matter had no beginning, it could claim the same honour as God. But God needs nothing already there, and no help, in order to create. Even the earth and the waters were made out of nothing.

teaching.title: Father, Son and Spirit create together
teaching.text: Read with the rest of Scripture, the opening of Genesis shows the Father creating through his Word, with his Spirit over the waters. Christians have long seen the Trinity here: God the Creator, the Son as the Beginning in whom he made all things, and the Holy Spirit moving over the waters. Some are careful not to prove this from the grammar of the first verse, yet agree that it is right to read the eternal Spirit of God in this one. God’s Word and his Breath are at the origin of the being and life of every creature.

teaching.title: The Spirit gives life and holds creation in being
teaching.text: The hovering shows the Spirit preparing the waters to bring forth living things, and so taking an active part in making the world. There is a lesson for the present too: if even the first chaos needed God’s Spirit to keep it from falling apart, the ordered world needs him no less. Creation is not a machine that God started and left running. The creed shared by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches calls the Spirit the Lord, the giver of life.

teaching.title: The first creation points to the new creation
teaching.text: From the earliest centuries, Christians saw baptism in this verse. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at the beginning goes on resting over the waters of baptism, where people are born of water and the Spirit. The verse also speaks to the heart and to the last day: the power that brought a world out of confusion, emptiness and darkness is the power that makes a person new and will raise the dead.

differences.title: Spirit or wind?
differences.text: The Hebrew word can mean either. The early Church, the medieval teachers and the Reformers all read it as the Spirit of God, a reading they saw as confirmed by the oldest authorities, and some thought the idea of a mere wind not worth answering. Some Jewish interpreters read it as air or wind, and some modern translations follow them. Both readings were known and weighed, and Christian teaching has held to the Spirit.

differences.title: Was the earth formless for a time?
differences.text: Some early teachers held that the unformed state came first in time, and was then shaped over the six days. Others held that it came first only in the order of nature, not in time. Since God can make a finished thing in an instant, the two views turn out to differ only a little. Both have been held freely in the Church.

differences.title: Where the traditions put the weight
differences.text: Orthodox teaching leans on the early sermons on the six days, which remain its classic reading of this chapter. Catholic teaching hears the verse at baptism: at the Easter Vigil, the blessing of the water recalls that at the dawn of creation the Spirit breathed on the waters and made them a source of holiness. Protestant teaching stresses the Spirit’s power to sustain the world and to give new birth. These are differences of emphasis, not of doctrine.

verses.simple:
God speaks for the first time, and light appears. One word, and the darkness over the deep gives way.

There is no delay. God says let there be light, and there is light. His word does exactly what it says.

Light comes first so that everything else can be seen. From this moment, the works of God are no longer hidden in the dark.
verses.context:
Genesis 1:2 left the earth formless, empty and dark, with God’s Spirit over the waters. Now, for the first time in the account, God speaks. Verses 3 to 5 make up the first day: God makes light, sees that it is good, separates it from the darkness, and names the day and the night.

This is the first of the works by which God sets things apart and gives the world its shape. Notice that light comes before the sun, moon and stars, which only appear on the fourth day.

The first day came to matter to Christians in another way too. It was the first day of the week, the day on which Christ rose from the dead early in the morning. And Paul looks back to this verse when he describes God shining in human hearts.
verses.meaning:
Early Christian preachers loved to picture this moment. With one word, light sprang through the whole world in an instant, north and south, east and west. The darkness vanished, the waters grew clear and sparkling, and everything took on a sweet and gracious look.

They were careful about what God’s speaking means. It is not a sound made with breath and tongue. It is the simple sign of God’s will, and the command was itself the deed. What God intended and what came to be matched exactly: a word, and a world.

Your Bible may word this differently. The older Catholic English Bible, following the Latin, has God command that light be made, and then says that light was made. The repeated words make the same point: what God says, happens.

Why light first? Not so that God could see to work, since darkness and light are alike to him. He made it so that we might see his works, and his glory in them.
verses.theology:
God’s word is power. When God speaks, it is done, truly and for good, not in show only. Christians see in this verse the eternal Word, the Son. By him the light was made, for in him was light, and he is the light of the world.

Light comes from God, not from the sun. God made light before the sun and moon. We easily tie God’s power to the means he uses, as if there could be no light without them. The order of the days shows that he holds the light in his own hand.

The God who made light makes light in us. Paul says that the God who called light out of darkness has shone in our hearts. At the beginning God said, let it be; in Christ he himself became our light. Because God made light shine in the darkness by his Word, he can give the light of faith to those who do not yet know him. When a person turns from darkness back to God, it is as though he says again, let there be light.
verses.today: As daylight comes this morning, or when you switch on a lamp tonight, let it remind you of the first word God spoke. Notice one thing the light lets you see, and give thanks for it.
verses.question: Where in my life am I still waiting for God to say, let there be light?
verses.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
verses.title: In the beginning.
verses.reflection: Read the words slowly, in the passage around them.

words.meaning: The plain Hebrew word for light. On the fourth day the sun and moon are called by a word built from it: lights, or instruments of light. They carry and spread a light that God had already made.

echoes.text: seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
echoes.note: Paul looks back to this verse: the God who called light out of darkness has shone in our hearts, in the face of Christ.

echoes.text: The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world.
echoes.note: Christ, the Word by whom the first light was made, is himself the true light.

echoes.text: For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
echoes.note: Those who were once darkness are now light in the Lord: this verse happening again in a human life.

echoes.text: This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
echoes.note: God is light, and the light of creation is meant to lead us to him.

teaching.title: God’s word does what it says
teaching.text: The first word of God made light, scattered the gloom and lit up the world in an instant. God’s speaking is not a sound in the air but the sign of his will, and his command was itself an action. He spoke, and it was done, really and lastingly. Christ is the eternal Word, and by him the light was produced.

teaching.title: Light comes first so his works can be seen
teaching.text: It was fitting that light should be made before everything else, because light is what makes all other things visible. With it the work of setting things apart begins, and the beauty of the world can be seen. God did not need light to see by. He made it so that we could see his works and his glory in them, and work our own works while it is day.

teaching.title: God holds the light in his hand
teaching.text: It was no accident that light came before the sun and moon. We are quick to tie God’s power to the means he uses, as though there could be no light without the sun. By the very order of creation, the Lord shows that he holds the light in his hand and can give it without them. On the fourth day he simply appoints the sun, moon and stars to spread a light he had already made.

teaching.title: The same word brings light into the heart
teaching.text: Paul hears this verse in the gift of faith: the God who said light should shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts. At creation God said, let it be; but in Christ he did not merely speak, he himself became light for us. In the new creation, the first thing God works in the soul is light. When people grieve over their darkness and turn to God, it is as if he says again, let there be light, and there is light.

differences.title: Bodily light, or spiritual light too?
differences.text: Some early and medieval teachers read this first light as also the forming of the angels: spiritual creatures who became light by turning toward the Word and cleaving to him. Others held that the account passes over the angels and speaks only of the light of the visible world. Some said the angels were left out because they were made before, others because a people prone to worship the sun and stars might have worshipped them too.

differences.title: How could there be days before the sun?
differences.text: Some early preachers taught that the first light itself spread out and drew back by God’s measure, making day and night. Medieval teachers questioned this, and thought the first light was the sun’s own light, not yet given its final form. Others, among the Reformers, left such details undecided as not very necessary to know, and stressed instead what the order of the days teaches about God.

verses.title: Rest that makes room for life.
verses.simple:
The Lord is the speaker's shepherd, and here he says what that care looks like. God has settled him in a place of green grass, and fed him beside water where he can rest.

The sheep does not find this place on its own. The shepherd brings it there. Rest, in this psalm, is something received from God's hand.
verses.context:
Psalm 22 in your Bible is the Shepherd psalm, numbered Psalm 23 in many other Bibles. Its heading and its first line share verse 1, so this is the second thing David says about the Lord as his shepherd.

David had been a shepherd before he was king, and he knew how much a flock needs a good one. The psalm has no complaint in it. It is pure thanks and trust. It moves from pasture and water to a restored soul, through the shadow of death, to a table, oil and a cup, and a home in the house of the Lord.

It comes straight after the psalm that begins with the cry, why have you forsaken me. Some Christian teachers read the two together: first Christ dying for his sheep, then his people receiving his care.
verses.meaning:
A good shepherd knows that sheep need grass, water and shade. Fast streams are hard for them to drink from and can do them harm, so he leads them to rich grass and gently flowing water. The rest here is the rest of a flock that is fed, settled and safe.

Your Bible says there he has made me dwell, where many Bibles say he makes me lie down. The Hebrew word for the pasture may also mean a shepherd's lodging, a shelter from the heat of the sun, so a meal and a home sit close together in this line.

Your Bible also says he has nourished me by the water of rest. The psalm book of early Christian preachers said: by the water of refreshing he has brought me up. They heard in the green place a pasture that leads to faith, and in the water of rest the water of baptism, which refreshes those who have lost their health and strength.
verses.theology:
God stoops to be our shepherd. It is a lowly, homely picture, and one who stoops so low for us must love us very much. He is a shepherd to those who know their weakness. Even David, a powerful king, called himself a poor sheep.

Rest is a gift, not a prize. God makes his people lie down, and gives them quiet and contentment whatever their lot. He gives refreshment as well as food and rest, and he does it for his own name's sake, not for their merit.

Early Christian preachers heard this as the psalm of the newly baptized. The green place leads to faith, and the water of rest is the water of baptism. The newly baptized sang it on their way to the altar, and heard in the table, the oil and the cup the Eucharist and the seal of the Spirit.

Christ is the Good Shepherd. In the Church, the psalm is the voice of the Church speaking to Christ. The Shepherd of the whole people is also the shepherd of each believer, and no one is too small for his care.
verses.today: Notice one moment today when you are fed or refreshed without earning it: a meal, a glass of water, a quiet minute. You might let it be a small sign that rest can be received.
verses.question: Where am I trying to find my own pasture, instead of letting myself be led?

words.meaning: Pastures, or fields of rich grass. Some translate it as lodgings for the shepherd: shelters set up in good grazing land to shield the flock from the summer sun.
The Hebrew verb behind lie down in many Bibles. It means to lie down or to repose, and it may also hint at the shelter of the shepherd's lodging.

echoes.text: He shall tend his flock as a shepherd, and he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and shall soothe them that are with young.
echoes.note: God tends his flock like a shepherd, and even the least of his sheep is not beneath his notice.

echoes.text: Attend, O Shepherd of Israel, who guidest Joseph like a flock; thou who sittest upon the cherubs, manifest thyself;
echoes.note: The Shepherd of all Israel is also the shepherd of every single believer.

echoes.text: He chose David also his servant, and took him up from the flocks of sheep.
echoes.note: David was taken from following the flock, so he knew a good shepherd's care from the inside.

echoes.text: And I will go in to the altar of God, to God who gladdens my youth: I will give thanks to thee on the harp, O God, my God.
echoes.note: The newly baptized said these words as they hurried to the altar, then sang the Shepherd psalm.

echoes.text: Go, eat thy bread with mirth, and drink thy wine with a joyful heart; for now God has favourably accepted thy works.
echoes.note: Bread and wine eaten with joy, and oil on the head, were heard as hints of the psalm's table, cup and anointing.

teaching.title: God stoops to be our shepherd
teaching.text: A shepherd is a lowly, homely picture, yet God often takes this name for himself in Scripture. One who stoops so low for our sake must love us very much. God is a shepherd to those who feel their weakness and are willing to stay in his fold. David, rich and powerful as he was, still owned himself a poor sheep, so that he might have God for his shepherd.

teaching.title: Rest is a gift, not a prize
teaching.text: It is God who makes his people lie down. He gives them quiet and contentment of mind, whatever their lot, and their souls are at ease in him, which makes every pasture green. He gives them not only food and rest, but refreshment too. And he does it not for their merit, but for his own name's sake.

teaching.title: The psalm of the newly baptized
teaching.text: Early Christian preachers heard in this psalm the whole path of a new Christian. The green place leads to faith, and the water of rest is the water of baptism. The newly baptized came to the altar singing this psalm. The table was the holy table God prepares, the oil was the seal placed on the forehead, and the cup was the cup Jesus took, gave thanks over, and called his blood.

teaching.title: Christ is the Good Shepherd
teaching.text: Prayed in the Church, the psalm becomes the Church speaking to Christ: the Lord Jesus Christ is my shepherd. Jesus seems to point back to it when he calls himself the good shepherd. The Shepherd of the whole Church is also the shepherd of each believer, and no one is too small for his care.

differences.title: Daily bread, or the mysteries of the Church?
differences.text: Some read the grass and water as the plain gifts of this life: the food, drink and shelter God gave David. They prefer to keep the next lines inside the shepherd picture too. Early Christian preachers heard faith, baptism, the seal of anointing and the Eucharist. Others hold both: daily bread from God's hand, and the green pasture of his word and worship, where the soul is fed.

differences.title: Lie down, or dwell?
differences.text: Some take the Hebrew word as pastures of grass where the flock lies down. Others read it as lodgings for the shepherd set in rich grassland, where the sheep could shelter from the heat. Your Bible, which says God has made me dwell there, sits close to that second picture.

verses.title: A prayer at the end of the day.
verses.simple:
These are the last words of the psalm. After a troubled day, the speaker lies down and sleeps in peace, because the Lord alone keeps him safe.

His peace does not come from a quiet world. It comes from God. Nothing around him has changed, but he has given his cares to the Lord, and so he can rest.
verses.context:
Psalm 4 is a prayer of David. In your Bible its heading counts as the first verse, so these words close the psalm as verse 9. Many other Bibles number them verse 8.

The psalm opens with a cry for help from someone hemmed in by trouble. Then David turns to people who love emptiness and chase lies, and asks how long they will be slow of heart. He calls them to search their hearts upon their beds, to offer right sacrifice and to trust the Lord. Many around him ask who will show them anything good. His answer is the light of God's face, which has put gladness in his heart.

The psalm may come from the long years when David was a hunted fugitive, though it was also written for God's people to pray. It ends with him quietly going to sleep, sure that God protects him by night as well as by day.
verses.meaning:
The peace of this verse is the gladness of the verse before, carried into the night. Early Christian teaching says that gladness is not found outside, in grain and wine and oil, but within, where the light of God's face is stamped on the heart. A soul pulled in many directions by wanting more cannot rest. A heart that seeks God simply can.

In your Bible the speaker will both lie down and sleep, and the Lord only makes him dwell securely. The psalm book used by early Christian preachers read: in peace, together, I will sleep. One early reading took that word together as pointing to God himself, who is always the same. The same Bibles ended the verse: you have made me dwell in hope.

The sleep here is first the sleep of a safe night. But it is also, some taught, a picture of the final rest.
verses.theology:
Real peace comes from God's favour. Many people want more grain and wine. The psalm points instead to the light of God's face. Early Christian teaching says that gladness is found within, where God's light is stamped on the soul like a king's image on a coin. True joy is God's gift, and no harvest can match it.

God alone is enough to keep us. The speaker sleeps as safely on his own as if a great company kept watch around him. Even when no human help can be seen, those under God's hand are kept in peace. A believer who has handed his cares to God can lie down like a farmer who sows his seed, then sleeps while it grows.

A divided heart cannot rest. Chasing many passing things pulls a person apart. God is always the same and never changes, and in him is a rest that forgets all labour.

Tonight's sleep points to the last rest. The verse looks ahead: I will sleep. Early Christian preachers saw here the perfect peace hoped for after this life, when death is swallowed up in victory. And because the Lord has already settled us in hope, that rest is sure.
verses.today: Before you sleep tonight, you might name the cares of the day to God, one at a time, and then leave them with him. Rest can begin before every problem is solved.
verses.question: What would I like to hand over to God tonight, so that I can lie down in peace?

words.meaning: A Hebrew word meaning alone, or apart. Some join it to God, as your Bible does: you, Lord, only, keep me safe. Others join it to the speaker: I live alone, and yet I am safe. Read that way, it answers the word together earlier in the verse.

echoes.text: I lay down and slept; I awaked; for the Lord will help me.
echoes.note: In the psalm just before, David had already lain down, slept and woken, and so he will sleep again.

echoes.text: Love righteousness, ye that be judges of the earth: think of the Lord with a good (heart,) and in simplicity of heart seek him.
echoes.note: Seeking God in simplicity of heart is the singleness that this verse's last line points to.

echoes.text: For the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthy tabernacle weigheth down the mind that museth upon many things.
echoes.note: A mind weighed down by many things is the opposite of the single, restful heart.

teaching.title: Real peace comes from God's favour
teaching.text: When many people ask who will show them anything good, they usually mean more grain and wine. The psalm points instead to the light of God's face, and to the gladness he puts in the heart. That gladness is not found outside, early Christian teaching says, but within, where God's light is stamped on the soul like a king's image on a coin. True joy is God's gift, and not even the joy of a rich harvest can match it.

teaching.title: God alone is enough to keep us
teaching.text: The speaker sleeps as safely on his own as if a great company kept watch around him, because God himself guards him. Even when no help from people can be seen, those under God's hand are kept in peace and safety. Having handed his cares to God in faith and prayer, a believer can lie down like a farmer who has sown his seed: he sleeps and rises, and the seed grows, though he does not know how.

teaching.title: A divided heart cannot rest
teaching.text: People who chase many passing things are pulled apart by them. Full of anxious thoughts, they cannot see the one simple good. Early Christian teaching sets that crowd of desires beside the first believers, who were of one heart and one soul. God is always the same and never changes, and in him is a rest that forgets all labour. So there is no need to run after the many things that are not God.

teaching.title: Tonight's sleep points to the last rest
teaching.text: Early Christian preachers noticed that the verse speaks of the future: not I have slept, but I will sleep. They saw in it the perfect peace that no tumult can break, hoped for after this life, when death is swallowed up in victory. Yet the verse also says the Lord has already settled the speaker in hope, and where that hope is now, what is hoped for will surely come. Some also read it at the end of life: a believer can lie down in death as Simeon departed in peace, trusting God to keep soul and body safe.

differences.title: Together with whom?
differences.text: Some read the word together as pointing to God himself, the One who is always the same. Others take it to mean that the speaker sleeps as safely alone as if a great crowd surrounded him. Others again thought his enemies would be reconciled, so that he could sleep among them in peace.

differences.title: Who is alone?
differences.text: Your Bible joins the word alone to God: the Lord only keeps me safe. Some Protestant readers join it to the speaker, who is alone and yet safe, and feel that the contrast with together is lost otherwise. Others hold both thoughts at once: though I am alone, I am not alone, for the Lord alone is enough.

differences.title: Sleep tonight, or the last rest?
differences.text: Some early Christian preachers read the sleep mainly as the perfect rest hoped for after this life, and stressed the future tense. Protestant teachers read it first as present quiet under God's protection, and some extend it to the believer's death.

verses.title: Hope with room for sadness.
verses.simple: The speaker feels deeply troubled and still turns toward hope. Faith does not require pretending to feel cheerful. Longing and trust can exist in the same prayer.
verses.context: The psalm describes thirst for God, tears, memories of worship with others and the pain of feeling forgotten. The speaker returns to a repeated address to his own soul. Read that refrain beside the laments around it.
verses.meaning: The repeated call to hope does not make the sadness disappear from the song. It creates a rhythm of remembering and turning toward God while the struggle continues. The poem gives language to a person who longs for connection and worship.
verses.theology:
Within Christian prayer, lament is a way of bringing suffering into relationship with God. A question such as “why?” can belong inside that relationship.

Hope here is directed toward God and future praise. It is not a prediction of when circumstances will change, and it does not make sadness a moral failure.
verses.today: You might recall one place, practice or person that has helped you feel connected. Reaching out for company can be a small response to the psalm’s longing for worship and community.
verses.question: What helps me stay connected when hope feels distant?

verses.title: Gratitude rooted in remembered care.
verses.simple:
The psalm opens with Alleluia, praise the Lord, and then a call: give thanks to the Lord. Two reasons follow. He is good, and his mercy lasts for ever.

The rest of the psalm shows why people can say this. Some were lost in the desert, some were in chains, some were sick, and some were caught in a storm at sea. They cried to the Lord, and he helped them. This first line is the song of thanks they sing afterwards, and the psalm invites everyone to sing it with them.
verses.context:
In your Bible this is Psalm 106. In Bibles that follow the Hebrew numbering it is Psalm 107.

The opening line was a familiar refrain in Israel's worship, and the psalm before this one starts with the same words. It seems that one side of a choir would sing, and the other side would answer: give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.

The psalm then tells four stories of trouble: people wandering in the desert, prisoners in darkness and chains, the sick drawing near to death, and sailors in a storm. Each follows the same pattern. They cry to the Lord, he saves them, and a refrain calls them to thank him for his mercies. The psalm ends by asking who is wise enough to notice these things and understand the mercies of the Lord.
verses.meaning:
Your Bible opens with Alleluia, a Hebrew word kept in the Greek, meaning praise the Lord. Many Bibles translated from Hebrew do not have it here. Early Christian preachers already knew that copies differed over where such an Alleluia belonged, and they kept the Church's custom of reading it with the psalm it heads.

Where your Bible says give thanks, early Christian preachers read confess. That word holds two things: owning up to our sins, and owning God's praise. To thank him because he is good is already to confess him.

He is good means good in himself, with no mixture of evil, the fountain from which every good thing flows. Early preachers also heard the word as sweet, and only someone who has tasted can say that.

His mercy endures for ever. His mercy is not for a season. It is shown to people now so that they may live with him for ever.
verses.theology:
Thanks grows from mercy we have tasted. This psalm is sweetest to those who have known God's mercy in their own lives. It was written for the whole people of God, so that they could see themselves in it as in a mirror.

We give thanks for his mercy, not for our own strength. In every rescue, it is his mercies that are praised. It is easy to cry to God in danger and forget him once we are safe.

Remembering gives hope in hard times. Calling past mercies to mind eases grief over present troubles and keeps the heart from despair. Nothing pleases God so much as a thankful heart, and we can thank him for blessings we see and for those we never noticed.

Thanksgiving is shared. When we are not in trouble, others are, and we give thanks for their help as well as our own. Thanksgiving marks the whole prayer of the Church.
verses.today: Think back over the past week and name one moment when help came, whether straight from God or through another person. Say thank you for it, aloud or in your heart. If someone near you was helped, you might give thanks for that too.
verses.question: What mercy have I already tasted that I have not yet stopped to thank God for?

words.meaning: A Hebrew phrase meaning praise the Lord. The Greek keeps the Hebrew words, joined into one. Where it heads a psalm, it serves as a title rather than as part of the psalm's text.
For he is good: good in himself, with no mixture of evil, and the fountain from which every good, and nothing but good, flows.
The Greek phrase behind for ever. God's mercy is not for a time only; it rests on people now so that they may live with the angels for ever.

echoes.text: Alleluia. Give thanks to the Lord; for he is good: for his mercy endures for ever.
echoes.note: The psalm before this one opens with the same line, and the two psalms belong closely together.

echoes.text: Alleluia. Give thanks to the Lord; for he is good: for his mercy endures for ever.
echoes.note: Another psalm begins with the same words, and then calls people to say that his mercy endures for ever, as the redeemed are called to say it here.

echoes.text: I will bless the Lord at all times: his praise shall be continually in my mouth.
echoes.note: Alleluia is sung on some days, but praise is meant to be in the mouth of the heart every day.

teaching.title: Thanks grows from mercy we have tasted
teaching.text: This psalm commends the mercies of God proved in our own lives, and so it is sweetest to those who have known them. Early Christian preachers said that only one who has tasted can confess that the Lord is sweet: if you have tasted, confess it. The psalm was written not for one or two people but for the whole people of God, so that they might know themselves in it as in a mirror.

teaching.title: We give thanks for his mercy, not our strength
teaching.text: After every rescue the psalm sings the same refrain. Let not our merits, our strength or our wisdom give thanks, early Christian preachers said, but his mercies; let him be loved in every deliverance who was called on in every distress. Protestant teachers warn how easily people cry to God in danger and then forget him once they are safe. To stay silent after such help would hide the wonderful works of God.

teaching.title: Remembering gives hope in hard times
teaching.text: The call to praise God for his goodness is also a call to remember. Calling past mercies to mind eases grief over present troubles and keeps the spirit from sinking into despair; it belongs to faith to celebrate God's mercy even in the hardest times. Early Christian preachers taught that nothing pleases God so much as a thankful person, and that giving thanks in comfort is nothing great. We can thank him for blessings we see and for those we do not, since he gives many without our asking or knowing.

teaching.title: Thanksgiving is shared
teaching.text: When we are not in trouble ourselves, others are, and we give God the glory for their deliverance too, because we are members of one another. We are to acknowledge his goodness to others as well as to ourselves. Catholic teaching says that thanksgiving marks the prayer of the Church, above all as she celebrates the Eucharist, and that every event and need can become an offering of thanks.

differences.title: Confessing sins, or confessing praise?
differences.text: The psalm before this one opens with the same line and goes on to say that we have sinned with our fathers, so some hear a confession of sins in it. Others hear chiefly praise in the words for he is good. Early Christian preachers held the two together: a confession of sins is only a holy one when it is made with praise of God and with hope in his mercy.

differences.title: For ever, or to the end of the world?
differences.text: Some read his mercy is for ever as the mercy without which no one can be happy, and that mercy never ends. Others read it as the mercy shown to people in misery, which lasts to the end of the world, since there will always be someone in need of it. Both readings were weighed by early Christian preachers.

differences.title: Who are the redeemed?
differences.text: Some read the redeemed as exiles, captives and travellers brought safely home, and see in the psalm God's care for all people, not only Israel. Others read them as the Church gathered from the whole world and set free in baptism, as Israel passed through the Red Sea. Some hold both: the psalm speaks of rescue in this life, and may also be applied to all who are saved by Christ.

verses.title: Belonging before achievement.
verses.simple:
This verse asks us to know three things. The Lord is God. He made us, and we did not make ourselves. And we belong to him: we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.

So belonging here does not begin with anything we achieve. It begins with being made. And the one who made us does not leave us to fend for ourselves. Like a shepherd with his own flock, he feeds and keeps what he has made.
verses.context:
In your Bible this is Psalm 99. In Bibles that follow the Hebrew numbering it is Psalm 100. Its title calls it a psalm for thanksgiving, and it is only five verses long.

The psalm calls the whole earth, not one nation alone, to shout for joy to the Lord, to serve him with gladness and to come before him. This verse gives the reason for all that joy. Then the psalm invites the people in through his gates with thanksgiving, and it ends: the Lord is good, and his mercy is for ever.

Because it calls every land, Christians have long heard in it the Church gathered from all the nations. It was made to be sung, and many still sing it often when they gather to worship.
verses.meaning:
To know that the Lord is God is more than agreeing that a god exists. It means giving him his full honour and setting nothing beside him. Early Christian preachers heard even more here: the Lord whom people mocked, struck and nailed to the cross is this same God, the one who made us.

Your Bible says he made us, and not we ourselves. That is the wording of the ancient Greek translation, and early Christian teachers in both East and West quoted the verse that way. Many Bibles translated from Hebrew read instead he made us, and we are his. In Hebrew the two readings differ by a single letter. Read together, they say one thing: because he made us, and we did not make ourselves, we are not our own but his.

The last line joins two pictures. We are his people, and we are his sheep. The many sheep make one flock. And this flock is not only owned but fed: they are the sheep of his pasture, the ones he takes care of.
verses.theology:
We did not make ourselves, so there is no room for pride. Another made us, and it is good for us to let him also make us whole. All of creation, the early Church taught, says the same thing to anyone who listens: we did not make ourselves, but were made by the one who lasts for ever.

We are his creatures by nature and his children by grace. As the works of his hands we are his servants. Yet the Son became as we are, so that we might receive his Spirit and dare to call our Lord Father. We are servants because we were made, and free because we are loved.

The Shepherd seeks and keeps his flock. He left the ninety-nine to find the one, and carried it home on his shoulders. The Church is the flock God promised to shepherd himself, fed and led by Christ, who gave his life for his sheep.

Belonging opens into thanksgiving. Confess that you did not make yourself, and praise the one who made you. That confession is the gate by which the flock comes in, and the praise will never end.
verses.today: Notice one moment today when you feel you have to earn your place. Pause there, and say the verse quietly to yourself: he made me, and I am his. Then carry on with your day as one of his flock.
verses.question: Where am I still trying to make myself, instead of resting in being his?

words.original: kai ouch hēmeis · καὶ οὐχ ἡμεῖς
words.meaning: The wording of the ancient Greek translation, which your Bible follows. The ancient Syriac and Latin translations agree with it.

In the Hebrew text, one letter changes the sense. As written, the word means not: he made us, and not we ourselves. As read aloud in the Hebrew tradition, it means his: he made us, and we are his. Many Bibles translated from Hebrew follow the second.

echoes.text: For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand.
echoes.note: Another psalm uses the same words, and there too the people and the sheep are one and the same flock.

echoes.text: Open to me the gates of righteousness: I will go into them, and give praise to the Lord.
echoes.note: Early Christian preachers read this beside the next verse: those who know who made them go in through God's gates confessing and praising him.

echoes.text: Begin the song with thanksgiving to the Lord; sing praises on the harp to our God:
echoes.note: This psalm says to begin with thanksgiving; the gates in the verse after ours are that same beginning.

teaching.title: We did not make ourselves
teaching.text: Early Christian preachers asked what reason we have for pride, since another made us, and the one who made us also suffered at our hands. It is good for us to let the one who made us also make us perfect. All of creation, they taught, says the same thing to anyone who listens: we did not make ourselves, but were made by the one who lasts for ever. Protestant teachers add that almost everyone admits God made them, yet people still make a god of themselves when they claim for their own power what belongs to God alone.

teaching.title: Creatures by nature, children by grace
teaching.text: Because God made us, we are his works and, by nature, his servants. Yet out of love for us the Son took a servant's form and became as we are, so that we, receiving the Spirit of the Son, might dare to call our Lord Father by grace. Early Christian preachers put it simply: you are a servant because you were created, and free because you are loved by the God who made you. His service is sweet, because all of us have been redeemed.

teaching.title: The Shepherd seeks and keeps his flock
teaching.text: The sheep of his pasture are not left to themselves. Christ the Shepherd left the ninety-nine to seek the one, and carried it home on his shoulders, ransomed by his own blood. Catholic teaching calls the Church the flock God himself promised to shepherd, fed and led by Christ, the Good Shepherd, who gave his life for his sheep. Protestant teachers stress that the same grace which first made us his also keeps us safe to the end.

teaching.title: Belonging opens into thanksgiving
teaching.text: Knowing whose we are is the start of worship. Early Christian preachers urged: confess that you were not made by yourselves, and praise him by whom you were made. That confession is the gate by which the flock enters, so that it is not left outside as prey for wolves. A day will come when there is no more confession of sins, but the confession of praise, that he is God and we are his creatures, goes on for ever.

differences.title: Not we ourselves, or we are his?
differences.text: The Hebrew text carries two readings that differ by one letter: he made us, and not we ourselves; or, he made us, and we are his. The ancient Greek, Syriac and Latin follow the first, as your Bible does, while some later scholars prefer the second. Some keep the familiar wording, saying the meaning is not altered. Others join the two: because God made us, and not we ourselves, we are not our own but his.

differences.title: Made as human beings, or made new?
differences.text: Many read he made us of creation itself: God formed our bodies and is the Father of our spirits, and we are his works by nature. Some Protestant teachers read it instead of being made new, the second birth by which God shapes his people for himself, a far greater gift than simply being born human. Early Christian preachers held the two close together: the one who made us is the Word through whom all things were made, and it is good for us to let him also make us perfect.
